blocks.text: During a 2024 appearance on ⟦1⟧ Brown recalled asking her parents for another dog when she turned 18, only to be told there wasn’t enough room.
I was living with them, then when I turned 18 I was like, ‘I want another dog,’ ” she said. “And they were like, ‘No, you can’t fit any more dogs in your room.’

Rather than give up on the idea, Brown moved next door and began creating a home that could accommodate her growing collection of animals. Although the property might sound like a peaceful retreat, the actress has been open about the reality of caring for so many pets while balancing her acting career.

Never miss a story — sign up for ⟦1⟧ to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.
You think this place is peaceful. But there’s so much chaos,” she told Vanity Fair. “My animals are loud, and it’s messy and my dogs are crazy.

Still, Brown has made it clear that the busy environment is exactly what she enjoys, describing her home as a place filled with laughter, excitement and activity.

“There is so much chaos, and that is where I thrive,” she said.

items.title: Joey’s Friends
items.text: Millie Bobby Brown runs Joey’s Friends, an animal rescue group based at her farm in rural Georgia.

items.title: Dog rescue
items.text: She and her team take dogs from local shelters, care for them, and give them temporary homes until they are adopted.

items.title: March 2026 gala
items.text: In March 2026, Brown held the group’s first annual gala to raise awareness for rescue dogs and the importance of second chances.

blocks.text:
⟦1⟧ has made a name for herself in Hollywood, but outside of acting, she’s devoted much of her time to a different passion: rescuing dogs. Since moving to a farm in rural Georgia in 2022, the ⟦2⟧ star has launched her own animal rescue organization, Joey’s Friends, where she and her team care for dogs in need of permanent homes.

The actress, 22, takes a hands-on approach to running the rescue. It focuses on taking dogs out of local shelters and fostering them until they’re ready for adoption. In a February 2025 interview with ⟦3⟧, Brown said she had been studying veterinary care so she could treat the animals herself.

“I’m able to treat wounds, take their pulse, moderate blood pressure, things like that. I do all their medical records myself,” she told the outlet, adding that her next step was completing an externship involving veterinary procedures.

⟦1⟧ also said that helping rescue animals takes more than sharing adoption posts online. “Adoption campaigns [on social media] are wonderful temporarily, but you really have to get in there and do the work to make a difference,” she said.

According to the ⟦2⟧, the group focuses on ⟦3⟧ that have faced abuse, neglect, or the risk of being put down in overcrowded shelters. The team gives them a safe place to stay and works on each dog’s physical and emotional needs before matching them with a family.

In March 2026, Brown marked another big moment for the group when she hosted its first annual gala. The event brought supporters together to highlight why animal rescue matters. In an ⟦4⟧ post, she wrote about how much the night meant to her and to the mission she is building.

Last night we hosted the first annual gala for my dog rescue. It was an incredible evening filled with community, compassion, and purpose,” she wrote. “Most importantly, we raised awareness for rescue dogs and the importance of second chances.

Along with the dogs she fosters, Brown also shares her Georgia property with her own pets and farm animals, including cats, goats, a donkey, a pony, a sheep, and a rabbit. She lives on the farm with her husband, ⟦5⟧, and has said before that wanting to care for more animals was a major reason she moved out of her parents’ home.
